TESTIMONY TO THE HOUSING AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT COMMITTEE
WRITTEN TESTIMONY IN FAVOR OF L.D. 1995 "AN ACT TO REQUIRE THE MAINE OFFICE OF COMMUNITY AFFAIRS TO ESTABLISH A TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE MATERIALS HUB"
DATE OF HEARING: JANUARY 8, 2026
Honorable Senator Chip Curry, Honorable Representative Traci Gere, Distinguished Members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee:
The Maine Association of Regional Councils (MARC) is writing in favor of L.D. 1995 "An Act to Require the Maine Office of Community Affairs to Establish a Technical Assistance Materials Hub." This legislation will establish a centralized technical assistance hub within the Maine Office of Community Affairs (MOCA), improving access to resources that support municipal and regional planning.
MARC represents Maine's Regional Planning Commissions and Councils, which are statutorily charged with building local government capacity, developing regional solutions to shared challenges, and serving as a link between municipalities and the State. Our member organizations are governed by and directly accountable to the municipalities they serve. MARC has previously supported the efforts of the Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future to create and establish MOCA and the subsequent actions by the legislature to support MOCA's ability to centralize guidance, funding opportunities, and support for municipalities that increases the efficiency by which Regional Councils can serve their member communities.
A centralized technical assistance materials hub reduces duplication of effort across state, regional, and local partners by providing consistent and accessible guidance to all communities. It improves equitable access to technical assistance for municipalities with limited staff capacity and strengthens regional councils' ability to support their members using current, reliable tools. The hub also creates a clear pathway for regional councils to contribute locally developed resources and lessons learned, allowing effective approaches to be shared more widely. By consolidating information on emerging trends, proven strategies, and relevant funding opportunities, the hub supports more efficient coordination and better alignment of state resources with local and regional needs.
Sincerely,

hub would save time, reduce duplication of effort, and help local leaders focus their energy on
- implementation rather than research. When communities can find off-the-shelf tools that help them

everyone benefits.

Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development, my name is Matt Marks, and I am a Principal at Cornerstone Government Affairs, testifying on behalf of the Associated General Contractors of Maine in support of LD 1995, "An Act to Require the Maine Office of Community Affairs to Establish a Technical Assistance Materials Hub."
Why contractors support LD 1995
LD 1995 requires the Maine Office of Community Affairs to create and manage a centralized hub for technical assistance materials that provide communities with information and tools on planning, climate resilience, housing, and development.
From a contractor's perspective, this is exactly the kind of practical, "one-stop" resource that can:
� Help municipalities, especially small and rural towns, access consistent and current technical guidance instead of relying on outdated documents or ad hoc advice;
� Improve the predictability and quality of project planning, which reduces change orders, delays, and cost overruns during the design and construction phases; and
� Support better alignment between local planning goals and state and federal requirements, particularly for housing, climate-resilient infrastructure, and community facilities.
The bill's language envisions the hub including:
� Best-available projections, models, assessments, and data related to planning, climate resilience, housing, and development;
� Tools that help visualize regions and communities and integrate data;
� Libraries of white papers, case studies, research articles, and best practices;
� Information on funding opportunities; and
� Regionally prioritized best-practice projects that support collaboration.
For contractors in the field, these elements translate into clearer expectations up front and fewer surprises after communities secure funding and move into design and construction. Better

information at the planning stage is one of the most cost-effective investments the Legislature can make.
Coordination with practitioners "on the ground"
As you move LD 1995 forward, we encourage you to ensure that the Office of Community Affairs continues to coordinate closely with practitioners, including:
� General contractors and specialty subcontractors;
� Design professionals; and
� Municipal officials and code enforcement officers.
Having contractors at the table as the hub is built will help ensure the materials are not only technically sound but also practical, constructible, and realistic in the Maine marketplace.
Ensuring alignment with the Buy America Build America Act
As communities increasingly rely on federal funding, compliance with the Buy America Build America Act (BABA) is no longer optional; it is a central project risk.
Under BABA, for federally assisted infrastructure projects, iron, steel, manufactured products, and construction materials generally must be produced in the United States, with strict domesticcontent standards for components and manufacturing processes. These requirements are being actively implemented and refined by federal agencies, and non-compliance can jeopardize funding, delay projects, or force costly substitutions late in the process. Maine's housing goals will be hindered by compliance requirements.
Because LD 1995 explicitly contemplates that the hub will provide tools, case studies, and information on funding opportunities, it is critical that any materials, tools, or product-related content in the hub be aligned with BABA.
We respectfully recommend the committee:
1. Direct the Office of Community Affairs to include clear guidance on BABA/Buy America compliance within the technical assistance materials hub, including:
o Plain-language summaries of applicable domestic-content requirements;
o Links to current federal guidance, waiver information, and agency-specific interpretations; and
o Sample procurement/contract language communities can use to document compliance.
2. Ensure that any model specifications, product examples, or "recommended" equipment or materials highlighted in the hub are reviewed for BABA compliance, or are clearly labeled when:
o The example assumes a federal waiver or exemption; or

3. Encourage coordination with industry and suppliers so that the hub's content reflects what is actually available in the domestic market and incorporates emerging guidance from agencies like FHWA, EPA, HUD, and others as they operationalize BABA.
4. This approach will help municipalities avoid a situation where a technical assistance document directs them to products, assemblies, or design choices that seem good on paper but are not BABA compliant, which could lead to costly redesigns or reprocurements later. Aligning the hub with BABA from the start will protect taxpayers, minimize risks for contractors, and strengthen the case for federal investment in Maine communities.
Regular updates and long-term value
LD 1995 already requires the Office of Community Affairs to regularly update the hub. That provision is especially important for BABA and other federal requirements, which are evolving as agencies issue guidance, waivers, and rulemakings. Building in a structured update process, ideally with ongoing input from contractors and other practitioners, will ensure the hub remains a trusted, living resource rather than a static website that quickly becomes outdated.
On behalf of Maine contractors, I urge you to give LD 1995 an Ought to Pass recommendation, with the clear expectation that:
� Practitioners, including contractors, will be involved in shaping the hub; and
� Any product-related tools, examples, or guidance included in the hub will be reviewed for consistency with Buy America Build America Act requirements or clearly labeled where exceptions apply.
Thank you for your time and for your work to strengthen Maine's communities. I would be happy to answer any questions or to participate in stakeholder discussions as the Office of Community Affairs implements this important tool.

Chair Curry, Chair Gere, and members of the Committee on Housing and Economic Development:
On behalf of the Maine Affordable Housing Coalition (MAHC), I am writing in strong support of LD 1995.
LD 1995 is a practical proposal that addresses a challenge we hear throughout Maine: communities lack accessible, consistent, centralized technical guidance to help plan for and implement housing projects.
From the perspective of affordable housing advocates, this kind of shared, up-to-date technical resource is essential infrastructure for housing production. Maine needs to ramp up its housing production to meet its goals, and this will help support that. In recent years, Maines's Legislature has enacted important land-use and housing reforms designed to expand by-right development and reduce regulatory barriers. However, many communities, particularly small and rural municipalities with part-time or shared staff, lack the capacity and expertise to fully implement these reforms.
Communities need support to leverage new housing laws and understand how they interact with existing zoning, subdivision review, and comprehensive plans. In some cases, communities delay or discourage housing proposals - not because they oppose housing, but because they lack guidance on how to apply state law or implement best practices used successfully elsewhere in Maine. This uncertainty adds time, cost, and risk to housing development and can stop projects before they ever get started. LD1995's new hub would help address these gaps.
Importantly, LD 1995 does not mandate local action or impose new requirements on municipalities - it empowers communities with information and tools, enabling better outcomes with existing staff and resources. At a time when Maine urgently needs more housing of all types, we must pair policy reform with practical implementation support. LD 1995 does exactly that, strengthening local capacity and helping ensure that housing goals translate into real-world results.
For these reasons, the Maine Affordable Housing Coalition respectfully urges the Committee to vote Ought to Pass on LD 1995.

Maine Transit Association Supports LD 1995 An Act to Require the Maine Office of Community Affairs to Establish a Technical Assistance Materials Hub
Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development January 8, 2026
Good Morning Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development. My name is Megan Hannan, and I am here today on behalf of the Maine Transit Association (MTA), which represents public transit providers across the State of Maine, including urban, regional, and rural systems operating a wide range of vehicle types.
MTA supports LD 1995 and the creation of a centralized technical assistance materials hub to help communities successfully plan and implement housing and economic development projects. We respectfully urge the Committee to ensure that public transportation and mobility considerations are explicitly included in the scope of materials developed under this legislation.
Our recommendation is straightforward: the materials hub should include transit and transportation plans, agency contacts, and route information so that municipalities, planners, and developers can consider mobility needs early in the development process.
As housing development has accelerated across Maine, transit providers are increasingly encountering projects where siting decisions are made without early consideration of how future residents will access jobs, schools, health care, groceries, and other essential services. Too often, transportation is treated as a secondary consideration rather than a core element of housing feasibility.
While undeveloped or lower-cost land located outside town and job centers may appear attractive from a development perspective, these sites frequently lack meaningful transit access. This challenge is increasingly consequential given the convergence of state housing reforms, including reduced parking requirements, the expansion of workforce and income-restricted housing, and federal policy frameworks that condition access to critical programs such as Medicaid/MaineCare and SNAP on work, job training, or volunteer participation for certain populations. When housing is sited without early consideration of transportation access, residents may face structural barriers to meeting these requirements, even when employment or qualifying activities exist within the broader region.
In addition, recent changes in state housing policy that encourage or require greater intown or in city residential density will, by design, reduce reliance on private vehicles and increase the need for alternative transportation options. In many cases, density requirements and reduced parking allowances will necessitate greater use of transit services even for short trips within municipalities. At the same time, housing developed in rural or lower-density areas presents a different but equally important

challenge, where longer distances and fewer transportation options can exacerbate access barriers if transit is not considered early. Transit infrastructure will necessarily take different forms depending on population density, geography, and local travel patterns, and will require coordination among municipalities, project developers, and transit providers to be effective.
Transit access should be evaluated at the same early stage as other essential infrastructure--such as water and sewer, electricity, broadband, and stormwater--rather than addressed after siting decisions have already been made. Including transit and mobility resources in the technical assistance materials hub would help communities make more informed, coordinated decisions and support housing that is both affordable and truly accessible.
Thank you for the opportunity to testify. MTA appreciates the Committee's leadership on housing and economic development and looks forward to supporting the successful implementation of this legislation.
I am happy to answer any questions you have.
Megan Hannan, Director of Government Affairs & Community Engagement, Greater Portland Metro Vice Chair, Maine Transit Association mhannan@gpmetro.org | 207.831.9893

Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and distinguished Members of the joint standing committee on Housing and Economic Development, my name is Samantha Horn, Director of the Maine Office
of Community Affairs. I am testifying in support of LD 1995, An Act to Require the Maine Office of
Community Affairs to Establish a TechnicalAssistance Materials Hub.
The Maine Office of Community Affairs, or MOCA, was created in 2024 to foster communication
and partnerships between the State and communities in this State. Our charge is to engage with municipalities, tribal governments and regional councils to provide coordinated and efficient planning, technical assistance and financial support to better plan for challenges, pursue solutions and create stronger, more resilient communities.
Communities across Maine are contending with increasingly complex challenges including housing shortages, climate effects from extreme storms, and planning for new land uses that pose
unique challenges. To help communities navigate, MOCA proposes to create a Technical
Assistance hub. This resource hub will provide a user-friendly searchable database for a variety of technical assistance materials to assist communities, policymakers and the public with planning and implementation efforts. Currently, the technical assistance materials that exist are spread
across many different state government agencies and community partner websites, which is a source of frustration for community staff and volunteers and the service providers who assist
communities. The hub would create a one-stop shop for up-to-date resources.
ltwill be a searchable database of land use planning, climate, housing, and other technical
assistance resources that are organized by subject matter. The type of resources we intend to
include are:
o Assessments, plans, and strategies 0 Communication or education materials

o Planning and/or policy guidance o Data, tools, research
o Case studies, projects, or examples
Materials would come from the MOCA programs and from federal, state, regional, nonprofit,
industry, academic, and local partners.
We have already begun background wor|< in anticipation of this project. in 2025 MOCA contracted
with the Southern Maine Planning and Development Commission to inventory land use planning and housing technical assistance documents from state, regional, and local partners. With a grant
from the Maine Community Foundation, we are continuing that work by hiring a part-time
contracted project managerforfour months to expand and prioritize the inventory of resources, identify high-priority additional resources that should be created, and find out from potential users what features they most need from this hub.
We are particularly interested in legislative support for this concept so we can document for future
legislatures and Administrations that this is a key need and so we can explain to our partners who
will contribute to this toolthat the product will be durable and their time and efforts are well-
spent.
For these reasons, I respectfully request your support for LD 1995. Thank you foryourtime, and I
am happy to answer any questions you may have.

The Maine Office of Community Affairs (MOCA) is a valuable step forward for planning in Maine; it will increasing statewide coordination, consistency, and sharing of planning resources and best practices.
The MAP LPC is made up of municipal planners, regional planners at state Regional Planning Organizations, and planning consultants working across the state on topics such as land use, housing, economic development, mapping, code revisions, and comprehensive planning.  improve coordination amongst numerous state programs;  increase efficiency of state programs;  offer clarity for Maine towns about who to call with questions; and  provide effective structure and staffing of existing state programs.
The Technical Assistance Materials Hub directly enables MOCA to achieve these above goals by offering a centralized clearinghouse of planning information, data, analysis, and mapping tools. Having this information curated by one office and available in one location reduces confusion about which data sets to use, for example, and helps communities across the state make efficient and effective planning decisions. This Hub will greatly improve consistency, coordination, and communication of planning information and data for Maine communities and RPOs.
Sincerely,
The Maine Association of Planners Legislative Policy Committee
